title: Minesweeper
summary: A flood-fill and lazy-generation case study — mines are placed only after the first click, so you can never lose on move one.

slides.markdown:
The Minesweeper prompt has an obvious trap: it's tempting to spend your design time on grid rendering and click handling — UI concerns — instead of the model underneath. The interviewer wants `Board`, `Cell`, and the reveal algorithm; the UI is assumed.

The two ideas that actually carry the interview: **flood-fill** reveals a whole region of safe cells in one action instead of one cell at a time, and mines are placed **only after the first click**, so the player can never lose on move one.

Think of the board as a graph where adjacent zero-mine-count cells are connected — that's what flood-fill traverses.

**In scope:** a grid of configurable size with a configurable mine count, two player actions — **reveal** a cell and **flag** a cell as a suspected mine — and a win condition: every non-mine cell has been revealed. Losing means revealing a mine.

**Non-goals** unless asked: a scoring/timer system, difficulty presets beyond grid size and mine count, and multiplayer. One requirement worth confirming explicitly: mines must not be placed until *after* the first reveal, so the very first click is always guaranteed safe — this is a real rule in the original game, not an interviewer trick, and it drives a specific design decision (§ the hard part).

Three entities. **Cell** holds three independent pieces of state: whether it's a mine, whether it's revealed, whether it's flagged, plus its computed adjacent-mine count. **Board** owns the 2D grid of cells and the reveal/flag operations. **Game** tracks win/loss and the count of cells still needing reveal.

The modeling decision worth naming: a cell's mine status and its revealed/flagged status are **independent booleans**, not one enum — a cell can be a mine and flagged and unrevealed all at once, or safe and revealed. Collapsing these into a single state enum (like `HIDDEN_MINE`, `FLAGGED_SAFE`, ...) explodes into 2^3 combinations for no benefit over three plain flags.

<<< Image: class diagram for Board and Cell — Cell showing three independent boolean fields (isMine, isRevealed, isFlagged) plus an adjacentMineCount int, Board showing a 2D array of Cells and methods reveal(cell) and toggleFlag(cell), Game showing a reference to Board and a remainingSafeCells counter >>>

Notice `Cell` has no method that decides game outcome — it's pure state. `Board.reveal()` is where the flood-fill logic lives, and `Game` is the only place that decides win or loss.

slides.sectionTitle: The hard part: placing mines after the first click
slides.markdown:
If mines are placed at board construction — before any reveal — the first click can hit one, ending the game before it starts. Real Minesweeper never does this, and getting it right is a genuine design decision, not a minor detail.

The fix: construct the board with **no mines placed yet**. On the *first* `reveal(cell)` call, generate the mine layout — excluding the clicked cell (and often its neighbors, for a bigger guaranteed-safe opening) from eligible mine positions — then compute every cell's adjacent-mine count, and only then proceed with the normal reveal logic.

This means `Board` needs an explicit `isFirstMove` flag, and `reveal()` branches on it before doing anything else.

<<< Image: 2D grid diagram showing a flood-fill in progress — a cluster of zero-count cells already revealed and shaded, with an arrow-and-queue visualization showing the frontier of cells about to be visited next, and numbered cells at the boundary that stop the fill from propagating further >>>

The fill only spreads through the shaded zero-count region; the numbered boundary cells get revealed once (since they're neighbors of a zero cell) but never enqueue their own neighbors.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: recursive flood-fill vs iterative BFS/queue
slides.markdown:
| | Recursive flood-fill | Iterative BFS with an explicit queue |
|---|---|---|
| Code shape | Direct, reads like the algorithm description | Slightly more code — manual queue management |
| Stack depth | One call frame per cell in the connected zero-region | None — state lives in the queue, not the call stack |
| Risk on huge boards | A very large open region (e.g. a 200x200 board with few mines) can exhaust the call stack | No stack-depth risk regardless of region size |

**How to decide:** recursive flood-fill is fine, and more readable, for typical board sizes (9x9 up to ~30x30). For a genuinely large or unbounded board size, prefer the iterative BFS version — naming this trade-off unprompted is a strong signal in the interview.

A hexagonal grid, or a board with irregular holes cut out of it, changes exactly one thing: what counts as a "neighbor." A square grid's `getNeighbors(cell)` returns up to 8 surrounding cells; a hex grid's returns up to 6, in a different coordinate scheme (axial or offset coordinates); an irregular board's simply excludes missing cells.

Because `reveal()`, the flood-fill recursion, and `computeAdjacentCounts()` are all written purely in terms of `getNeighbors(cell)` — never in terms of raw row/column arithmetic — none of that code needs to change. Only `getNeighbors` itself is board-shape-specific.

This is the same lesson as generalizing win-lines in Tic-Tac-Toe or regions in Sudoku: isolate the one shape-specific piece, and everything built on top of it is free.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: re-scanning the whole board to check for a win
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "After each reveal, I'll loop over every cell and check whether all non-mine cells are revealed to detect a win."

**Why it's wrong:** it's the same class of mistake as recomputing a win-check from scratch in Tic-Tac-Toe or re-validating the whole Sudoku grid after one placement — a full-board scan after *every single reveal* is needless repeated work, and it gets slower as the board grows, right when performance matters most (a big board with a large opening flood-fills dozens of cells in one action, each potentially triggering a full rescan).

**Correct model:** track a **remaining-safe-cells counter** on `Game`, decremented once per successful non-mine reveal. The win condition is simply `remainingSafeCells == 0` — an O(1) check after any reveal, including a flood-fill that reveals many cells at once.
